definition: Incarnate means existing in bodily or human form.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word incarnate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know incarnate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: To the harbor crews the old pilot was reliability incarnate, first aboard in any weather for forty years.
Symbolic is the faintest form — a thing merely stands for the idea — and stops far short of incarnate, where the idea walks around in a body.
Personified gives the idea a human face in art or speech, but stops short of incarnate, which claims the idea is actually present in flesh.

Embodied is the cool, general word for an idea given concrete form — a policy embodied in a document, a value in a ritual — and no flesh is required. Incarnate makes the stronger, stranger claim: the quality itself has taken on a living body.

Corporeal simply means having a physical body — flesh rather than spirit — and any creature qualifies. Incarnate runs the claim the other way: not that a being has a body, but that an abstraction like greed or patience has stepped into one.

Incarnate usually stands after its noun — greed incarnate, patience incarnate — and it claims more than resemblance: in- ('in, into') + caro, carnis ('flesh') says the quality itself has taken on a body.

The first thing every new stagehand learned at the Orpheum was to watch for Vera Holt.
Vera had run the theater's backstage for thirty years, and the crew spoke of her as caution incarnate.
They did not mean she followed the safety rules.
They meant something stranger — that the rules seemed to have taken on a body and gone walking.
Ropes she passed tightened themselves, the joke went; trapdoors latched at the sound of her step.
Watching her cross the fly floor, you were not watching a woman think about care.
You were watching care itself, wearing boots.
When she retired, the crew did not say the theater lost its safest worker.
They said caution itself had walked out the stage door.
